items.title: First imaged black hole
items.claim: The Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a supermassive black hole in 2019. Which one?

options.text: Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way
The black hole at the centre of M87, around 53 million light-years away
A solar-mass black hole in Cygnus

items.reveal_title: M87* came first; Sagittarius A* followed in 2022
items.reveal:
EHT's M87* image released 10 April 2019; Sagittarius A* image released 12 May 2022. M87* is roughly 6.5 billion solar masses; Sagittarius A* is around 4 million.

EHT combines radio telescopes on multiple continents to create an Earth-sized aperture.
items.why: Imaging the largest objects in the universe required a planet-sized synthetic instrument.

items.title: What the universe expands into
items.claim: When cosmologists say the universe is expanding, what is the most accurate description of where it expands to?

options.text: The metric of space itself increases distances between unbound objects; there is no external 'outside'

items.reveal_title: Expansion is of the metric, not into a container
items.reveal:
General relativity describes the metric of space evolving with time. The FLRW metric encodes this expansion.

Gravitationally bound systems (galaxies, the Local Group) are not expanding with the cosmic flow.
items.why: Cosmology requires letting go of everyday intuitions about space as a fixed stage.

items.title: The Milky Way and Andromeda
items.claim: Andromeda (M31) is moving toward the Milky Way at about 110 km/s. When are current models predicting first close passage?
items.reveal_title: Around 4.5 billion years, plus or minus
items.reveal:
Cox and Loeb (2008) predicted a close passage around 4.5 billion years from now, with full merger over subsequent billions of years.

Gaia data have refined Andromeda's tangential motion since.
items.why: Galactic-scale events follow timescales that dwarf human history.
